newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Masood's men eager to move on Afghan capital.
newsitem.headline: Masood's men eager to move on Afghan capital.

text.p: Conditions for an Afghan ceasefire set on Monday by Ahmad Shah Masood, poised outside the capital Kabul, showed the former government military chief was in little mood to compromise.
"If a ceasefire is agreed today, then talks on the demilitarisation of Kabul should start immediately," said Dr Abdullah (one name), spokesman for the ousted government's top commander.

But the radical Islamic Taleban militia is unlikely to agree to pull its forces from the capital. The militant warriors, who are believed to control about three-fourths of the country, captured Kabul and ousted President Burhanuddin Rabbani on September 27.

Plumes of dust and smoke rose off the hills north of Kabul as Masood's Jamiat-i-Islami forces lobbed rockets and shells on Taleban positions along the new road which leads into the northeast of the city.

Jamiat fighters lounged along mud walls in the frontline village of Hussein Kot, 15 km (10 miles) north of Kabul, clutching assault rifles under a hot October sun. One soldier disappeared in a cloud of diesel smoke as a Russian-built tank roared into life.
They hardly flinched as a single Taleban shell smacked into the road a few yards away.

A crowd of well-armed fighters milling around outside Masood's headquarters in Jabal os-Siraj, one with a flower poked in the end of his gun barrel, shook their heads in the negative when asked if they wanted a ceasefire.
"We want to go forward," said one young fighter, shouldering a rocket-propelled grenade launcher.
Abdullah said government representatives were in talks with Uzbek chieftain Abdul Rashid Dostum in his northern base of Mazar-i-Sharif, along with the Pakistani interior minister, Naseerullah Babur.

But asked what Masood would do if the Taleban refused the government's conditions for demilitarisation, Abdullah said: "What is their (Taleban's) chance of staying in Kabul? They have no support from the people, they are under great pressure militarily, they have losses."
A western observer based in the region said of Masood's forces, "If they want to go for a military solution and take Kabul, they can do it. Masood is very strong now."
The roads up to the frontline on Masood's side are full of Jamiat fighters, reinforced with around a thousand extra troops from the Panjsher Valley on Sunday.
Two weeks ago, Masood's mainly Tajik fighters were driven back into their Panjsher Valley stronghold some 90 km (60 miles) north of Kabul, but hit back with some stunning counter-attacks.
His latest breakthrough came on Friday when, with the backing of Dostum's artillery, he took Bagram airbase some 50 km (30 miles) north of Kabul.

Late last week a Taleban evacuation of Kabul was floated at the United Nations. The United States called it "probably premature", although State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said a proposal to demilitarise Kabul was "an important idea".
Abdullah played down Monday's fighting, saying, "There are only small engagements at the moment. They (Taleban) still hold the (De Sabz) pass."

Further back along the main road into Kabul, refugees on trucks loaded with belongings began to trickle back into the small town of Charikar, retaken from the Taleban last week. A few men worked the fields, oblivious to the low boom of shelling on the hills above the valley.
